sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The domain of active strike-slip deformation in NW and W Slovenia is positioned between the S vergent thrust domain in the Friuli area of NE Italy and SW thrusting domain of the Dinarides. Earthquake and geology data in NE Italy indicate that the prevailing mechanism of deformation is thrusting on E-W oriented planes whereas dextral-reverse and purely dextral strike-slip displacements on NNW-SSE oriented planes occur further E and SE. The prevailing fault orientation in the Dinarides is in the orogen-parallel NW-SE direction. Earthquakes and geologic data along these faults exhibit thrust focal mechanisms in the southern and central parts of the Dinarides, and dextral-reverse mechanisms in the northern Dinarides.
The first stage of mountain building connected to the South Alpine orogeny is Eocene thrusting and reverse fault movements along the NE Adriatic margin. During the Eocene to Lower Miocene, NE-SW directed shortening led to thrusting and uplift along SW vergent NW-SE oriented faults in the Central and External Dinarides (e.g. Tari and Pamic, 1998; Pamic et al., 2002), Julian and Friuli Alps, and E Dolomites (Doglioni, 1987). The Eocene Dinaric faults were strongly dismembered by younger, mostly late Oligocene and Miocene, south-vergent South-Alpine thrusts and steep reverse faults, which resulted in overthrusting and refolding of Dinaric structures both in the Friuli region (Doglioni, 1987; Nussbaum, 2000) and in the Julian Alps (Placer and Car, 1998). During Late Oligocene-Miocene South Alpine shortening resulted in formation of E-W oriented thrust and reverse faults. During the Miocene-Pliocene transition, the Alpine region was subjected to a change in regional style of deformation probably due to termination of subduction and slab pull along the eastern edge of the Carpathians (Horvath and Cloetingh, 1996). This change in the regional stress field coupled with the continuous northward motion of Adria resulted in inversion and reactivation of previous favourably oriented structures. The NW-SE oriented faults were reactivated in a dextral strike-slip manner and continue to exhibit such kinematics with the ongoing deformation of 2 mm/yr towards NNE oriented horizontal velocy vectors recorded by GPS measurements (Grenerczy, 2002). The majority of regional seismicity is concentrated on N and E margins of the Adria and the region of W Julian Alps together with Friuli-Venezia Giulia, represents seismically most active area in the entire Alpine region. The Idrija Fault is responsible for the strongest event recorded in the region that occured on March 26th 1511, as well as an M 5.8 event of January 1st 1926. The Ravne Fault, that lies just 8 km to the north and exhibits same geometrical and mechanical characteristics as the Idtija Fault has hosted moderate sized earthquakes in 1998 and 2004 with magnitude values of 5.7 and 5.2 respectivately. Approximately 30 km to the E from this Source lies the source of the 1976 Gemona earthquake that occured on E -W oriented thrust plane.
This Source lies on the NW-SE trending, dextral strike-slip Idrija Fault that in its NW part runs through the eastern part of the Southern Alps, while at its SE end extends to the unit of Dinarides. The source extends along the strike of the Idrija fault system, that exhibits right-stepping segmentation along its trace. The northwestern boundary of the source is in the area of interaction between the E-W trending Gemona-Kobarid thrust with the NW-SE oriented strand of the Idrija Fault System. The activity of the south-eastern part of the source is testified by moderate historical and instrumental seismicity. The Mw 5.8 1926 Cerknica earthquake is located in the area of a segment over-step zone.
We set the depth interval of this Source based on data of local and regional geologic setting. We obtained the average strike on the basis of published geologic maps (Buser, 1986) and field and geomorphological observations. Average dip and rake were inferred from published work on local geologic conditions (Buser, 1986; Cunningham et al., 2006) and geomorphological data. Values of minimum and maximum slip rates were based on results of geodynamic modelling (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012) and geological considerations. Higher values for the minimum and maximum slip rates for the Idrija fault are reported by Moulin et al. (2014) based upon nalaysis of LIDAR data and geomorphologic considerations. Given that such values were obtained only based on surface data where all the other contributing relief shaping factors were not considered, we do not think they are representative of the seismogenic process along the Idrija fault. Maximum magnitude of the source was assigned after the March 26th 1511 earthquake (Rovida et al., 2011), that is strongest earthquake reported for the Idrija Fault as well as the region of eastern Southern Alps and northern Dinarides.

pictures.c: Regional location of the Idrija and Ravne faults with other major structural elements of NW Slovenia. The Idrija Fault system runs parallel to the Ravne Fault, that lies 8 km to the north and exhibits better rock exposure. To the NW, the fault exhibits a change in strike to WNW-ESE, and interaction with E-W oriented thrusts (after Kastelic [2008]).

pictures.t: LiDAR obtained images of a section of Idrija Fault
pictures.c: LiDAR obtained DEM ground surface model of the topography of a stratch of the Idrija Fault about 4.5 km to the NW of the town of Idrija. The revealed geomorphic features reveal indices of active tectonics connected to dextral strike-slip movements (after Cunningham et al. [2006]).

pictures.t: Recorded historical and instrumental seismicity for the region of NE Italy and W Slovenia
pictures.c: Recorded historical and instrumental seismicity for northeastern Italy and western Slovenia. The  northwestern reach of the Idrija Fault is shown with (a). Not much seismic activity is recorded along the trace of the fault in addition to the 1511 earthquake, that is generally associated with it (after Burrato et al. [2008]).

pictures.t: Long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides
pictures.c: Average long-term fault slip rates for the External Dinarides (Kastelic and Carafa, 2012). The width of each colored band is proportional to long-term slip rate. The blue and green bands represent thrust and dextral strike-slip faulting, respectively. The numerical values plotted above the fault traces are the average slip rates for each fault element. Each active fault is coded with its corresponding alphanumeric value.
